period: Generally placed among the earlier Upanishads, in the mid-first millennium BCE; dating is uncertain
summary: An Upanishad in three sections covering recitation and student ethics, Brahman as truth, knowledge and bliss, and the five 'sheaths' of the person.
whyRead: Taittiriya gives the classic 'five sheaths' (koshas) model of the person, moving from body to breath, mind, understanding and bliss, still used in yoga and Vedanta today. Its third section shows inquiry as a step-by-step discovery rather than a transmitted doctrine.
story: In the third section Bhrigu asks his father Varuna to teach him Brahman. Rather than answer, Varuna gives a definition and tells him to find out through austerity and reflection. Bhrigu successively concludes that Brahman is food, breath, mind and understanding, each time returning to be sent back, until he realises that Brahman is bliss.
questions: What is a human being made of?
What is the relation between Brahman and bliss?

keyTeachings.title: Truth, knowledge, infinity
keyTeachings.text: The second section opens by characterising Brahman as truth (satya), knowledge or consciousness (jnana) and the infinite (ananta). Advaita treats this as a definition of Brahman's essential nature.

keyTeachings.title: The five sheaths
keyTeachings.text: The person is described as layered sheaths made of food, breath, mind, understanding and bliss. Later Vedanta uses the scheme to guide attention inward to the Self beyond them.

keyTeachings.title: Bliss as the nature of Brahman
keyTeachings.text: The text ranks degrees of joy and presents Brahman as a bliss beyond words and thought.

keyTeachings.title: Learning through inquiry
keyTeachings.text: Bhrigu is not given the answer but led to discover it, which many teachers take as a model for spiritual education.

keyTeachings.title: Ethics of the graduating student
keyTeachings.text: The first section closes with advice to the departing student: speak truth, follow dharma, honour mother, father, teacher and guest.
